title: Hyper backend pauses for about 30 seconds between multiple URLs
body: I am fetching three flight-information URLs with curl on Windows 10. A build made with `-DUSE_HYPER` takes at least a minute, with long pauses between URLs, whether the URLs come from a config file or the command line and whether or not I use `--parallel`. The curl bundled with Windows completes the same three requests in under a second. My development build is curl 8.2.0-DEV with Hyper 1.0.0-rc.3. Updating Rust, pulling Hyper master, and rebuilding everything did not change the behavior.

symptoms_visible: My `-DUSE_HYPER` curl build pauses for a long time between three URLs and takes at least a minute overall.
Using `--parallel` does not remove the pauses, while the curl bundled with Windows finishes the same requests in under a second.
N0.label: N0 Hyper multi-URL slowness reported

symptoms_visible: After updating to the build with the early Hyper polling changes, my Hyper build still takes 61.321 seconds versus 1.515 seconds for the Windows curl.
Only two of the three expected response lines appeared in that run, and I have seen the first response disappear in some runs.
N1_x.label: N1_x early polling workaround aftermath

symptoms_visible: The default Hyper request still takes more than 60 seconds, but the same three URLs finish in about 300 milliseconds when I run them with `--http1.1`.
N2.label: N2 protocol-mode timing collected

symptoms_visible: The default Hyper run still has roughly 30-second pauses after the first response, while the explicitly selected HTTP/1.1 run is fast.
N3.label: N3 repeated HTTP/2 setup observed

symptoms_visible: After rebuilding the latest curl and Hyper sources, the three URLs complete in 0.974 seconds with no minute-long pauses; the Windows curl takes 0.803 seconds on the same run.
N_terminal.label: terminal long pauses resolved

solution.intent: Work around the delay by polling Hyper's executor again immediately after an empty result and applying the associated early Hyper-stream polling changes.
solution.concrete_example: Call `hyper_executor_poll` a second time when the first poll returns an empty task, so a response that became available during I/O processing can be consumed immediately.

edges.comment: Messages c2 and c7-c11: participant2's extra-poll experiment and early changes improved their own test, but the reporter's Windows system still took 61.321 seconds on an updated build and sometimes omitted a response. This reporter-side result falsifies the early polling workaround as the complete fix.

question_patterns: Can you time the same URLs while explicitly selecting each supported HTTP protocol mode and report the raw timings?
Does forcing a different negotiated protocol mode change the delay?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With the normal Hyper invocation the three URLs take more than 60 seconds. Running the same command with `--http1.1` takes about 300 milliseconds.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both the default invocation and the `--http1.1` invocation take more than 60 seconds with the same pauses.
The default invocation takes about 58 seconds and `--http1.1` takes about 400 milliseconds.

edges.comment: Message c23 on participant4's reproducing Linux system, folded into the affected-user side: the raw comparison was over 60 seconds by default and approximately 300 ms with `--http1.1`. The conclusion that the Hyper HTTP/2 integration is defective remains engineer-side.

question_patterns: Can you capture the traffic for both builds using an SSL key log and list the order of the protocol frames and requests you observe?
What frame sequence do you see on the connection for the three-request run?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: In Wireshark, the normal backend sends one HTTP/2 connection preface, settings and window update, followed by requests 1, 2 and 3. With Hyper I see a connection preface, settings and window update before request 1, then another preface and settings before request 2, and another preface and settings before request 3.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both builds send exactly one connection preface followed by all three requests; the frame sequences are the same.
The Hyper capture has the same repeated-preface sequence, but the settings and window-update frames appear in the opposite order.

edges.comment: Message c23 on participant4's reproducing system: this is the raw decrypted Wireshark sequence. Later participants c35-c41 interpreted it as a per-request Hyper client lifecycle problem that produces invalid HTTP/2 behavior.

solution.intent: Temporarily disable HTTP/2 in the Hyper backend so requests use the working HTTP/1.1 path, avoiding invalid repeated HTTP/2 connection setup until the Hyper integration can be redesigned around connection lifetimes.
solution.concrete_example: Build current curl with the temporary Hyper HTTP/2 disable, rerun the three-URL benchmark, and confirm that the 30-second pauses and missing responses are gone. Restoring Hyper HTTP/2 safely requires keeping the Hyper client connection for the connection lifetime, likely through a connection-filter design.
solution.inference_hint: The affected users supplied protocol timings and the raw frame sequence. Engineers concluded that curl created a new `hyper_clientconn` for every request on one HTTP/2 connection, causing repeated connection prefaces; servers could answer with GOAWAY, after which curl delayed, retried, or dropped a request. They selected disabling Hyper HTTP/2 as the safe short-term fix because persisting the client correctly conflicts with curl transfer and connection lifecycles.

edges.comment: Messages c35-c46: participant7 summarized the lifecycle and GOAWAY failure, proposed the temporary HTTP/2 disable, and explained that full restoration needs a connection-filter redesign. The reporter then rebuilt current curl on their Windows system and measured 0.974 seconds versus 0.803 seconds, with the original minute-long pauses gone. That post-landing verification is represented only in the terminal node.

solution.intent: Temporarily disable HTTP/2 in the Hyper backend and fall back to HTTP/1.1 because the integration creates request-scoped Hyper client connections that emit invalid repeated HTTP/2 setup on a reused connection.
solution.concrete_example: Use a current build in which Hyper HTTP/2 is disabled, then rerun the three URLs and verify that they complete without the long pauses. A later architectural fix can restore HTTP/2 by aligning the Hyper client lifetime with curl's connection lifetime.
solution.inference_hint: This shortcut represents an agent that already knows the accepted resolution. In the thread, the per-request client connection and repeated-preface diagnosis was established only after protocol timing, tracing, and packet capture.

edges.comment: Shortcut from the reporter's opening Windows report to the accepted short-term resolution from c35-c46. It exists because the first historical attempted remedy was later falsified; it allows an immediately correct proposal while explicitly marking the diagnostic evidence it skips.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the final accepted root cause: curl's Hyper integration created a Hyper client connection per request rather than per underlying connection, so an HTTP/2 connection received repeated connection prefaces and settings; server GOAWAY handling then produced delays, retries, or dropped requests.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: the default Hyper path takes over a minute while the explicitly selected HTTP/1.1 path takes about 300 ms, and the packet capture shows one preface for the normal backend but a new preface before every Hyper request.

The practical fix must disable HTTP/2 for the Hyper backend and use HTTP/1.1 until the integration is reworked around curl connection lifetimes; it must not imply that HTTP/2 itself is generally slow.
Must not present the earlier extra-executor-poll or small polling changes as sufficient, because the reporter still measured 61.321 seconds and sometimes lost a response after those changes.
Must ask the reporter to verify a current build before declaring resolution; the graph establishes successful verification at 0.974 seconds with no minute-long pauses.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical curl builder and tester on Windows; comfortable compiling curl, Hyper and Rust toolchains, switching TLS backends, writing batch reproductions, adding debug logging and inspecting assertion values, but not confident reasoning about Hyper's internal synchronization and lifecycle design.
persona_hint.communication_style: Direct and evidence-oriented; supplies complete commands, versions and timings, follows rebuild requests, and openly says when internal implementation details are outside their expertise.
